Technical definition: Relative clause about an inanimate plural
Informal explanation: those that X, see Focus tags in Nishnaabemwin high level explanation
KM suggestions: A relative clause about more than one inanimate thing. Similar to saying ‘those that’ (do something).
More than one inanimate thing is the object (thing acted on by verb). Similar to ‘those’ or ‘things’ in the English sentences, “She fixed those” or “She repairs things.”

Technical definition: Relative clause about an inanimate plural obviative
Informal explanation: those others that X, see Focus tags in Nishnaabemwin high level explanation
KM suggestions: A relative clause about inanimate things that have been backgrounded. Similar to saying ‘those other ones that’ (do something).
Multiple inanimate things that are the subject (doer or focus) of the verb (action) but are backgrounded or defocused like saying, “Those other ones float” instead of “They float.”
Inanimate nouns (things, those) that are the subject (doer or focus) of the verb (action) like in the English examples, “Those float” or “The things float.”

Technical definition: Relative clause about an inanimate singular
Informal explanation: the thing that Xes, see Focus tags in Nishnaabemwin high level explanation
KM suggestions: A relative clause about one inanimate thing (singular). Similar to saying ‘the thing that’ (does something).
When an inanimate singular noun is the object of a verb like ‘it’ in “I kept it.”

Technical definition: Relative clause about an inanimate singular obviative
Informal explanation: the other thing that Xes, see Focus tags in Nishnaabemwin high level explanation
KM suggestions: When a relative clause is about an inanimate singular noun (it, thing) that is backgrounded (obviated). Like, ‘the other thing that’ in “That thing and the other thing that plays music.”
When an inanimate singular noun that is backgrounded (obviated) is the subject. Similar to saying, ‘the other thing’ in “The other thing worked better.”
When an inanimate singular noun is the subject of a verb like ‘it’ in “It keeps time.”
Oneself, expressed by saying ‘I,’ or ‘me.’
When the first person (I, me, myself) is acted on by the verb like in the English example, “The dog jumped on me.”
When the first person (I, me, myself) possesses something. For example, “my house.”
Oneself (I) is the subject (doer) of the verb (action). For example, “I fish.”
Second person addressing a group (two or more) like forms in some varieties of English such as: youse/youse’s, y’all/y’all’s, you all/ you all’s, or you guys/you guy’s.
Two or more second persons (‘you guys,’ ‘y’all,’ or ‘youse’) are the object (thing acted on by the verb) like in, “I saw y’all.”
Two or more second persons (‘you guys,’ ‘y’all,’ or ‘youse’) possess something. For example, “You guys’ house.”
Two or more second persons (‘you guys,’ ‘y’all,’ or ‘youse’) are the subject (doer) of the verb. For example, “Y’all fish.”
Second person, you.
Second person, you as the object of the verb like in the English example, “I saw you.”
Second person (you) possesses something. For example, ‘your’ in “I like your dog.”
Second person is the subject (doer) of the verb. For example, “You camped up north.”
‘They’ or ‘the other guys’ like in the examples, “They fished” and “The other guys fished.”

Technical definition: Relative clause about a third person plural obviative
KM suggestions: A relative clause about a third person plural (they) that is backgrounded or defocused (obviated). Similar to saying, “the others who went.”
When a backgrounded or defocused (obviated) third person plural (they) is the object of a verb. For example, ‘the other ones’ in “I saw them and the other ones.”
When a backgrounded or defocused (obviated) third person plural (they) possesses something. Similar to saying, “the other guys’s.”
When a backgrounded or defocused (obviated) third person plural (they) is the subject (doer) of a verb. For example, ‘the other ones’ in “The other ones told me.”
A third person plural (they) that is the focus (proximate) while another third person is defocused like ‘they’ in “They helped those other guys.”

Technical definition: Relative clause about a third person plural proximate
KM suggestions: A relative clause about a third person plural (they) that is the focus (proximate) while another third person is defocused. Similar to ‘they who’ in “They who helped those other guys.”
When a third person plural (they) that is the focus (proximate) while another third person is defocused is the object of a verb. For example, ‘them’ in “I saw them and the other ones.”

When a third person plural (they) that is the focus (proximate) while another third person is defocused possesses something. For example, ‘their’ in “Their dog was nicer than those other guys’s dogs.”

KM suggestions: When a third person plural (they) that is the focus (proximate) while another third person is defocused is the subject (doer) of the verb. For example, ‘they’ in “They knew those other guys.”
Third person singular, ‘he,’ ‘she,’ ‘it.’

Technical definition: Relative clause about a third person singular obviative
KM suggestions: When a third person singular (s/he, it) is backgrounded or defocused in a relative clause. For example, ‘the other one who’ in “I want to thank her and the other one who helped.”
A third person singular (s/he, it) is backgrounded or defocused as the object of a verb. For example, ‘the other one’ in “I talked to him and the other one.”
When a backgrounded or defocused (obviated) third person (s/he, it) possesses something. Similar to saying, “the other guy’s.”
A third person singular (s/he, it) is backgrounded or defocused like saying ‘the other one.’
A third person (s/he, it) that is the focus (proximate) while another third person is defocused like ‘he’ in “He helped those other guys.”

Technical definition: Relative clause about a third person singular proximate
KM suggestions: A relative clause about a third person (s/he, it) that is the focus (proximate) while another third person is defocused. Similar to ‘the one who’ in “The one who helped that other guy.”
When a third person (s/he, it) that is the focus (proximate) while another third person is defocused is the object. For example, ‘her’ in “I saw her and the other one.”
When a third person (s/he, it) that is the focus (proximate) while another third person is defocused possesses something. For example, ‘his’ in “His car was newer than the other guy’s.”

KM suggestions: When a third person (s/he, it) that is the focus (proximate) while another third person is defocused is the subject (doer). For example, ‘he’ in “He and the other guy fish together.”
Words like ‘and,’ ‘or,’ and ‘but’ that link words, phrases, or clauses. ‘Miinwa’ and ‘gye’ are two common examples of coordinating words (coordinative adverbs) (Valentine 2001:996).
Adverbs expressing degree like, ‘really,’ ‘only,’ and ‘extremely’ (Valentine 2001:145).

Things like, ‘and,’ ‘so,’ or ‘then.’ For example, 
‘mii dash’ ‘and there’ (Valentine 2001:151).
Dubitative adverbs express hesitation or uncertainty, like ‘evidentially’ or ‘it seems’ (Valentine 2001:830-831).
Adverbs include time like ‘tomorrow’; location like ‘alongside’; manner like ‘barley’; circumstance like ‘on purpose,’ among other types (Valentine 2001:138-147).
Adverbs used in questions like ‘na’ for ‘yes/no questions’ (Valentine 2001:146).
Adverbs that express location or place like ‘here,’ ‘there,’ or ‘alongside’ (Valentine 2001:140).
Adverbs that express manner like ‘quickly’ or ‘thoroughly’ (Valentine 2001:142).
Negative adverbs can be words with negative meanings like, ‘at all’ or ‘ever.’ The other kind makes something negative (negation like not) (Valentine 2001:145).
Adverbs that connect more about the subject like ‘only later when’ (Valentine 2001:949).
Adverbs like ‘some,’ ‘all,’ ‘most,’ or ‘many’ (Valentine 2001:144).
Adverbs that express time such as ‘again,’ ‘today,’ ‘then,’ or ‘soon’ (Valentine 2001:140).

Informal explanation: preterit and dubitative: X has been completed and speaker doubts/needs to infer X
KM suggestions: A way of conjugating verbs to express doubt or hesitation about something that has been finished in the past (Valentine 2001:798-799).
First person plural excluding the listener (you), meaning we/us, not you.

Informal explanation: Y Xes us but not you
KM suggestions: The first person plural excluding the listener (you), meaning us, not you as the object. For example, “She called us (not you).”
First person plural excluding the listener (you) possess something, like saying ‘ours, not yours.’
We but not you do something. For example, “We (not you) are leaving tomorrow.”
First person plural like ‘we’ or ‘us’ including the listener. Like, ‘we (including you)’ or ‘us (including you).’
The first person plural (includes you) is the object, like in “She sent this for us (including you).”
First person plural including the listener (you) possess something, like saying ‘ours’ and ‘yours.’
First person plural inclusive, ‘us (including you)’ are the subject. For example, “We (including you) are invited.”

A person’s name.
The name of a place like ‘Bemidji.’

Informal explanation: more than one entity that has not been backgrounded by being obviated
KM suggestions: Persons or things (plural), they are the focus (proximate) rather than the backgrounded (obviative) persons or things.

Informal explanation: one entity, a third person that has not been backgrounded by being obviated
KM suggestions: A singular third person that is the focus (proximate) rather than the backgrounded (obviative) person or thing.

KM suggestions: On verbs in the independent order, the suffix has a temporal effect (something was completed). Verbs in the conjunct get a counterfactual (if something hypothetically were to happen) reading (Rice 2023).

Technical definition: Intransitive Verb with only PLural Animate subjects
Informal explanation: description/action of beings or remarkable things
KM suggestions: An intransitive verb (no object) with a plural animate subject.

Technical definition: Intransitive Verb with only PLural Inanimate subjects
KM suggestions: An intransitive verb (no object) with a plural inanimate subject like the verb, ‘mamaangaashkaa,’ ‘there are big waves’ (The Ojibwe People’s Dictionary).
